summary: Zero-cost abstractions, compile-time memory ownership, fearless concurrency, and bare-metal performance without a garbage collector.

rows.means: immutable variable binding by default / explicitly mutable binding
rows.consequence: Variables in Rust are strictly immutable unless declared mut, preventing accidental state corruption.

rows.means: function declaration with mandatory type signatures
rows.consequence: The last expression without a semicolon is the returned value. Statements ending in a semicolon evaluate to unit ().

rows.means: every value has exactly one owner; value moves when assigned
rows.consequence: let s2 = s1 moves ownership of heap data to s2. s1 is no longer valid, eliminating double-free memory corruption.

rows.means: references allowing reading / reference allowing writing
rows.consequence: The borrow checker's rule: any number of immutable references, or exactly one mutable reference, and never both at once. That single constraint is what makes a dangling reference and a data race both impossible to express.

rows.means: compile-time annotations proving references remain valid
rows.consequence: Ensures no reference outlives the data it points to, mathematically preventing dangling pointer bugs at compile time.

rows.means: type representing a value that may or may not exist
rows.consequence: There is no null pointer in the language. Absence is a value of the type, so the compiler can require that the absent case is handled before the value inside is used.

rows.means: type representing either operation success or failure with a reason
rows.consequence: All recoverable errors in Rust return Result. Combined with the ? operator for ergonomic error propagation.

rows.code: let file = File::open(path)?;   // returns Err to the caller
rows.means: unwraps Ok value or immediately returns Err upward to caller
rows.consequence: Replaces a match at every call with one character, while keeping the error type, so the short path and the careful path are the same path.

rows.means: exhaustive pattern matching expression
rows.consequence: The compiler guarantees that every possible enum variant or condition is handled; missing a case produces a build error.

rows.means: concise pattern matching when you only care about one variant
rows.consequence: Executes the block only if the pattern matches, ignoring all other possibilities without requiring an exhaustive match.

rows.means: associates methods and constructors with a struct or enum
rows.consequence: Functions without &self are associated functions (constructors like Type::new()); functions taking &self are instance methods.

rows.code:
trait TraitName { fn method(&self); }
impl TraitName for MyType { ... }
rows.means: defines a shared interface of behavior across types
rows.consequence: Behaviour is attached to a type after the fact rather than at its definition, and the call is resolved at compile time, so the abstraction costs nothing at run time.

rows.means: macro automatically implementing common trait behaviors
rows.consequence: Generates code at compile time for string debugging ({:?}), deep cloning (.clone()), or equality comparisons (==).

rows.means: heap allocation pointer with single ownership
rows.consequence: Moves data from the stack to the heap. Used for recursive types where the compiler needs a known pointer size at compile time.

rows.means: reference counting pointer for shared ownership, single-threaded and thread-safe
rows.consequence: The thread-safe version counts atomically, which is why it is the one that may cross threads and why it costs slightly more than the single-threaded one. Shared ownership is opt-in rather than the default.

rows.means: mutual exclusion primitive that encapsulates the data it protects
rows.consequence: In Rust, the lock protects the data itself: let mut data = mutex.lock().unwrap(); you cannot access the data without holding the lock.

rows.means: dynamically growable heap-allocated array
rows.consequence: Provides O(1) push and pop operations, continuous cache memory layout, and automatic deallocation upon dropping.

rows.means: zero-cost lazy iterator pipeline
rows.consequence: Compiles into machine code as fast as a handwritten C while loop, optimizing bounds checks away.

rows.means: heap-allocated owned string / borrowed read-only string slice
rows.consequence: The owned form can grow and change; the borrowed form is an immutable view into text that already exists somewhere else, which is why passing one costs nothing and returning one needs care about what it points into.

rows.means: permits raw pointer dereferencing and calls into other languages
rows.consequence: Used inside the standard library to implement the low-level primitives that the safe interfaces are built from. The block does not switch the checks off everywhere; it widens what is permitted inside it, and marks the region a reviewer has to read.
